1:
The Hebrew says in the field of the Philistines, and both Gill and Henry report a reading built on that before setting it aside. Gill cites Procopius Gazaeus for the notion that no city dared receive the ark, so it was left in the open air; Henry puts the same account to work, since if the ark stood in the fields it explains where the mice came from that destroyed corn nearly ripe — a judgment not mentioned in the previous chapter, so that Israel's enemies were cursed in city and field alike. Both prefer the ordinary sense of country, Gill following the Targum's cities and tracing the ark from Ashdod to Gath to Ekron. On the seven months he reckons back from the wheat harvest to place the battle at the end of autumn, and corrects Josephus, who makes it four months, contrary to the text.

The diviners draw the chapter's sharpest contrast in method. Clarke gives the root, to presage or prognosticate, and then stops: in what their pretended art consisted, we know not. Ellicott fills the same space with the practice of antiquity — diviners held a distinguished place in the counsels of every ancient nation under one name or another, magicians, sorcerers, soothsayers, augurs, oracles, plying their trade now with arrows, now with the entrails of slain animals, now with the stars, now with the flight of birds.

What the Philistines took themselves to be dealing with is judged differently. Ellicott is unsparing: the priests evidently thought the Hebrew Deity, somehow resident in the golden chest, a childish, capricious god like one of their own, who had been insulted, had proved powerful enough to injure his captors, and must now be appeased with rich offerings. Gill and Clarke find something sounder in the instinct. Gill allows they may have had some notion of a law in Israel, or spoken from the common heathen principle that deities are appeased by gifts; Clarke, following Calmet, generalises it — all people have held that though the Supreme Being needs nothing of his creatures he requires them to consecrate what they have, God himself commanding that none appear before him empty. Wesley defends the givers: these images were offered not in contempt of God, since they sought his favour, but in testimony of their humiliation, leaving a monument of their own shame that they might obtain pity.

On the images Gill canvasses three accounts — figures of the five cities, of a man with the disease, or of the afflicted part alone — then reports Maimonides, who attributes the word to them not for their outward form but for a spiritual virtue by which the disease was removed, making them a kind of talisman; and he adds Tavernier's report that Indian pilgrims still bring to a pagoda the figure of the affected member in gold, silver or copper according to their quality. Ellicott traces the same custom through the ancient world, shipwrecked men offering pictures or garments, gladiators their arms, captives their chains, and carries it forward without flinching to fifth-century Christians offering gold or silver hands, feet and eyes in their churches, and to the votive offerings still made in Roman Catholic countries. On the mice he supplies what the narrative assumes: this is their first mention in the Hebrew, though the Greek version had already appended the scourge to the account of the disease, and both Aristotle and Pliny record such devastations — in Egypt so dreaded that the mouse seems to have been the hieroglyph for destruction. Keil defends the priests' appeal to Pharaoh's hardening as perfectly natural, the report of those events having spread among all the neighbouring nations. Wesley reads give glory as a triad: the glory of God's power in conquering those who seemed to have conquered him, of his justice in punishing, and of his goodness if he relieves.
7:
Why the cart had to be new is answered three ways that do not quite agree. Clarke makes it a principle: it was indecent to employ in the worship of God anything that had served a common purpose, since to sanctify means to separate a thing from all earthly uses and devote it solely to God. Gill offers a practical reason first — there were no Levites or priests to carry the ark on their shoulders, so a cart was needed — and only then adds that it was new for the ark's honour. Ellicott quotes the Speaker's Commentary, which calls the arrangement a right and true feeling and lines it up with the colt whereon never man sat and the tomb wherein never man was laid, but then closes by pointing the reader to the supposed peculiar virtue of new things in the story of Samson's bowstrings — which is a quite different account of the impulse, and it is left standing beside the first.

How conclusive the test was they agree in substance and differ in what they stress. Clarke calls it a complete trial and gives the two independent improbabilities: unless supernaturally influenced the cows would not leave their calves, and unless supernaturally directed they would not leave home and take an unguided road they had never gone. Wesley adds the reason for choosing milch kine that had never borne a yoke, that such untamed heifers wander and keep no constant path as oxen used to the yoke do, and were therefore the least likely animals to hold the direct road; and he notes that removing the calves would stir the dams' natural affection homeward. Ellicott sets out both branches of the decision and, unlike the others, reports which way the diviners were betting: they felt quite sure the cows would return to their young unless driven by a divine power, in which case the Philistines might safely keep the ark and put their sufferings down to natural causes. Keil states the outcome against that expectation in a sentence — the God of Israel actually did what the idolatrous priests hardly considered possible.

The word rendered chance sets Clarke off on the most substantial note in the passage. The Hebrew, he says, comes from a root meaning to meet or coalesce and signifies an event arising naturally from such concurring causes as must in the order of things produce it — a bad state of the atmosphere, putrid exhalations, poor diet from a general scarcity, any of which might have produced this disease. That, he argues, is the proper notion of chance, and it shows the thing to be as dependent on divine providence as anything can be, such occurrences being parts of the divine government; the English word is often improperly used of what is outside that government, but is in itself simple and expressive, coming from the French for falling out, whence also the legal term escheat. Ellicott puts the same alternative more plainly, that the priests were not certain whether the plague came from the offended God of Israel or had visited Philistia in the ordinary course of nature.

Two smaller notes. Clarke corrects the translation of the gifts, since the word so often rendered jewels means vessels, implements or ornaments, and a jewel of gold has an odd sound to anyone who attaches the idea of a precious stone to the term. Ellicott points forward from the coffer set beside the ark, finding in the reverent awe with which these Philistines handled it a strong contrast to the careless curiosity of the men of Bethshemesh toward the same object — a curiosity punished, as acts of sacrilege so often are, with extreme severity.
10:
Henry reads the whole return as a second exodus, and works the parallel in two directions. God had fetched Israel out of the house of bondage, and now fetches the ark out of its captivity in such a manner that its captors were glad when it departed. First, they received no money or price for its ransom, though they had hoped for more than a king's ransom — as it was prophesied of Cyrus that he should let the captives go, not for price nor reward. Second, they gave jewels of gold to be rid of it, as the Egyptians gave to the Israelites, so that the ark which had been carried into Philistia as a trophy of their victory carried back trophies of its own and lasting monuments of their disgrace. From which he draws the general rule: God will be no loser in his glory by the successes of the church's enemies against his ark, but gets himself honour from those who seek to dishonour him.

The lowing of the cows is heard by three of them as the decisive detail, and Wesley states most exactly why. It testified at once both their natural and vehement inclination toward their calves and the supernatural power that over-ruled them to a contrary course — that is, the instinct is not suppressed but merely overborne, and the sound is the evidence. Clarke says simply that they were calling for their calves, and adds the circumstance some suppose, that the cart was set where two roads met, one to Ekron and one to Bethshemesh, so that the case might be the more certain. Ellicott makes the same point from the other end: the dumb beasts did what the idol priests and diviners scarcely thought possible, because God's hand drove them.

That the lords followed the cart is taken by two as part of the design. Clarke says they were so jealous in the business that they would trust no eyes but their own, and that all this was wisely ordered so that there might be the fullest conviction of the being and interposition of God. Wesley gives the same reason in fewer words, to prevent all imposture and get assurance of the truth of the event. Gill notices something that will matter later: these were Philistines who laid hands on the ark, and were not punished for touching it as Uzzah afterwards was, though an Israelite.

Ellicott alone comments on the manner of the telling rather than the events. The narrative throughout, he says, is evidently unadorned, very easy and natural, speaking of primitive customs and telling its story of divine interference with exquisite simplicity and truth — the dumb beasts going on their strange way with their golden burden, the princes of the Philistines following them, awe-struck, at a distance. Keil keeps to the sequence: the cart came to the field of Joshua the Bethshemeshite and stood still before a large stone, the townsmen chopped up its wood and offered the cows as a burnt offering, and meanwhile the Levites lifted off the ark with the chest of golden gifts. Wesley notes that Bethshemesh was a city of the priests, whose office it was to take care of the ark.
13:
Whether the sacrifice was lawful is raised by Wesley and answered uneasily. There may seem, he says, to be a double error in the act: that they offered females for a burnt offering, against the law's requirement, and that they did it in a place the law had not chosen. His defence is a concession: the case being extraordinary may in some sort excuse it, if they did not proceed by ordinary rules. Ellicott denies there was any irregularity to excuse. The offering of these sacrifices at Bethshemesh, though the tabernacle had never stood there, was no transgression of the law, because the ark was now present, the occasional throne of the glory-presence of the Eternal, before which the sacrifices were really offered. Clarke supplies a third motive that makes the question almost incidental: both cart and cattle, having been put to this use, could no longer be devoted to any secular service, so the cattle were sacrificed and the cart broken up for fuel to consume them. Keil leaves the legality alone and reads the meaning instead — in the burnt offerings they consecrated themselves afresh to the Lord's service, and in the slain offerings, culminating in the sacrificial meals, they sealed anew their living fellowship with him.

Ellicott makes the place itself the key to what follows. Bethshemesh, House of the Sun, was a priestly city, so it would have seemed a fitting home for the ark, Shiloh being now desolate. But the priests and Levites had forfeited their old position as guides and teachers of the people — the story of priestly life at Shiloh in Eli's last years showing how incapable the Levitical families were of influencing the people — and Bethshemesh was therefore no fit permanent dwelling for the ark. On his reading, the conduct of priestly Bethshemesh on this occasion is not to be wondered at: they rejoiced at first at the sight of their lost treasure, and then an act of careless irreverence called down a swift punishment.

Gill and Keil converge independently on a grammatical point. Both hold that the verse about the Levites taking down the ark is a supplementary remark to be read as a pluperfect, since the thing was done as soon as the cart arrived and before the burnt offering could be made with the cart's wood. Gill presses the identification further: those called Levites were priests, priests being of the tribe of Levi, and it was the priests' work to take the ark down though Levites might carry it — and he notes it as remarkable that Bethshemesh had been given to the Kohathites, whose charge was to carry the ark on their shoulders. Clarke states the plainer fact that some of the tribe of Levi were among the people there, and Ellicott adds that these were the principal men of the city, familiar with all the sacrificial rites.

Three smaller observations round out the passage. Gill dates the wheat harvest from Pentecost in the month Sivan, about our May, and draws from it that many were in the fields and so were eyewitnesses. Ellicott takes the great stone for a mass of natural rock rising from the soil, and makes it the reason the cart stopped where it did; of Joshua himself Gill can say only that we read of him nowhere else, and that whether he was a Levite — not improbable in a Levitical city — or a common Israelite is not certain. On the five golden emerods Ellicott fills a gap by inference: the previous chapter names only three cities as resting-places of the ark, but there is no doubt it was located for a longer or shorter period in each of the five, every one possessing a temple of Dagon. Clarke puts the same point administratively, that each city sent its emerod in what may be called its corporate capacity.
19:
The number smitten is the chapter's great difficulty, and Clarke and Ellicott both conclude the text cannot stand as it is. Clarke gives his grounds: the words are not naturally connected, they stand no better in the versions, and it is very improbable that so small a village should contain or employ fifty thousand and seventy men in the fields at harvest, much less that all could peep into the ark on one stone in a cornfield. He judges the text corrupt, or a word lost, or the fifty thousand added by ignorance or design, and shows the Latin version dividing the figures into seventy chief men and fifty thousand of the common people. Ellicott states as plainly that the present Hebrew, which the English follows literally, cannot be right. Wesley alone tries to save the figure rather than emend it, glossing of the people as those in and near Bethshemesh together with those coming from all parts on the occasion.

What the offence actually was is described three ways of increasing severity. Wesley is mildest: having an opportunity they never had before, it is not strange they felt a vehement curiosity to see the contents. Henry supplies the psychology of the forbidden — every Israelite had heard great talk of the ark and knew that even the high priest saw it but once a year, through a cloud of incense, which is just what makes men say what they would give for a sight of it; and he separates pretext from motive, since they lifted the covering under pretence of checking whether the Philistines had removed the two tables, but really to gratify a curiosity intruding into what God had thought fit to conceal. Ellicott reconstructs the scene and adds a circumstance no one else does: the chief men, most of them priests and Levites, heated with wine after the sacrificial feast, lost all reverence and resolved to gaze into the chest into which no profane eye in Israel had ever peered — wishing perhaps to see the grey Sinai tablets, perhaps excusing themselves by a desire to learn whether the Philistines had violated its secrets. He also rejects a rendering that would soften the charge, that they had merely looked at the ark with irreverent staring, preferring the received sense.

Their cry is judged very differently. Clarke is severe: they knew God had forbidden any but priests and Levites to touch the ark, and in this cry threw upon God, as a Being hard to be pleased, a blame belonging solely to themselves. Wesley agrees and makes it a rule: when the word of God works with terror on men's consciences they commonly quarrel with the word instead of blaming themselves. Gill allows both readings, a complaint of God's severity or a reverent acknowledgment of guilt, and adds that none can stand except through the mercy seat. Ellicott is the most generous: there is superstition in the cry, since they tied their invisible King too closely to a chest of wood and gold, yet through it he discerns a consciousness of sin that argued well for the reformation Samuel would soon bring about. He compares their fear to that of the apostle who fell as dead at the feet of the glorified Son of Man, and marks the difference: these had no Redeemer standing by to raise them.

Why they sent to Kirjath-jearim and not Shiloh is answered by inference. Clarke says it does not appear, and supposes Shiloh had been destroyed after the late defeat, which he thinks likely since the ark was never taken back there. Gill gives positive reasons — greater distance from the Philistines, greater eminence and strength — and leaves Shiloh open, suggesting Kirjath-jearim lay on the way there unless Shiloh was already destroyed; Wesley adds that Israelites would come more freely to such a place than to the enemy's border.
